plan.contextChunk: This figure places three small sketched graphs side by side, labeled (a), (b), and (c), each showing curves that rise from left to right on an unmarked vertical axis above a horizontal axis whose tip is labeled n; no numeric ticks appear anywhere. Panel (a) carries three curves: the highest is labeled c2 g(n), the lowest c1 g(n), and a third labeled f(n) weaves between them, dipping and crossing near the left edge before settling into the corridor between the other two. A dashed vertical segment drops from that crossing region to a tick on the n axis marked n0, and the expression f(n) = Theta(g(n)) is printed below the plot. Panel (b) has two curves, the upper labeled c g(n) and the lower labeled f(n); f(n) oscillates sharply at small n, meets c g(n) at the dashed line standing over the tick n0, and runs beneath it from there on, with f(n) = O(g(n)) underneath. Panel (c) reverses the roles, putting f(n) above and c g(n) below after they touch at the dashed n0 line, and is captioned f(n) = Omega(g(n)). Read against one another, the three panels turn on where the labeled curve sits relative to the scaled comparison function once n passes n0, giving the geometric intuition behind bounding a function from both sides, from above only, and from below only.

interactions.label: Asymptotic relation
interactions.teaches: Θ requires f(n) to be trapped between lower and upper constant multiples of g(n), O only requires an eventual upper bound, and Ω only requires an eventual lower bound

interactions.label: Threshold n0
interactions.teaches: Small-n behavior can violate the bound; the asymptotic claim only starts once n is at least n0

interactions.label: Constant multiplier on g(n)
interactions.teaches: Multiplying g(n) by a positive constant shifts the comparison curve up or down, so asymptotic bounds ignore fixed constant-factor differences

demo_steps.title: Two-sided Θ bound
demo_steps.narration: In the Θ view, f(n) must eventually stay inside a corridor between c1 g(n) and c2 g(n). Early crossings do not matter if they occur before n0.

demo_steps.title: Move the threshold
demo_steps.narration: Drag n0 to the right and notice that violations before the dashed line disappear from consideration. If a violation remains to the right of n0, the chosen threshold is not large enough.

demo_steps.title: Adjust the constant factor
demo_steps.narration: Changing the multiplier raises or lowers the scaled copy of g(n). A valid asymptotic bound often appears only after choosing a large enough positive constant.

demo_steps.title: Upper-only O bound
demo_steps.narration: In the O view, only the region below c g(n) matters after n0. f(n) may be much smaller than the bound; O does not require a matching lower bound.

demo_steps.title: Lower-only Ω bound
demo_steps.narration: In the Ω view, the allowed region is above c g(n) after n0. This is the mirror idea of O: f(n) must eventually be at least a constant multiple of g(n).

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Asymptotic notation is about eventual position relative to scaled copies of g(n), not exact equality and not behavior near the origin.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Recreate the original as three thin black sketched panels on a white background with no numeric tick marks. Put Θ on the left, O in the middle, and Ω on the right, each with a dashed vertical n0 line and the caption below the axis. Use subtle green shading for the active allowed region and small red marks for active violations to the right of n0. Keep inactive panels visible but slightly faded; the toggle should brighten the selected panel. The curves should look hand-drawn and smooth: f(n) wiggles and crosses near small n, then settles into the correct eventual relation after n0. The constant slider should vertically scale the labeled comparison curves while preserving their general increasing shape.

Figure 3.1(a) gives an intuitive picture of functions f .n/ and g.n/, where f .n/ D ‚.g.n//. For all values of n at and to the right of n0, the value of f .n/ lies at or above c1g.n/ and at or below c2g.n/. In other words, for all n _x0015_ n0, the function f .n/ is equal to g.n/ to within a constant factor. We say that g.n/ is an asymptotically tight bound for f .n/.
The ‚-notation asymptotically bounds a function from above and below. When
we have only an asymptotic upper bound, we use O-notation. For a given function g.n/, we denote by O.g.n// (pronounced “big-oh of g of n” or sometimes
just “oh of g of n”) the set of functions

We use O-notation to give an upper bound on a function, to within a constant
factor. Figure 3.1(b) shows the intuition behind O-notation. For all values n at and
to the right of n0, the value of the function f .n/ is on or below cg.n/.
Just as O-notation provides an asymptotic upper bound on a function, -notation
provides an asymptotic lower bound. For a given function g.n/, we denote

The generated panels are much taller and narrower than the source panels, making the curves look steep and compressed compared with the wide horizontal composition of the reference.

Several curve shapes differ noticeably from the source, especially the Θ panel where the upper c₂g(n) curve is drawn as a steep near-linear/parabolic boundary rather than the smoother S-like upper bound in the reference.
The generated figure adds extra pedagogical primitives absent from the source, including shaded allowed regions, active outlines, and potential red violation markers.
Inactive-panel labels and curves are low-contrast gray and quite small, whereas the source labels are all black and equally legible.
The x-axes include arrowheads in the generated figure, while the source uses plain axis lines with only the italic n label at the right.
